relationship: Blessed conduct defined by the Lord’s law
rationale: Psalm 118 opens by blessing those blameless in their way who walk in the Lord’s law. Psalm 1 likewise opens with a blessing, contrasts the sinner’s way with the blessed person’s conduct, and locates his will and meditation in the Lord’s law.

relationship: Seeking the Lord with the whole heart
rationale: The psalm blesses those who search the testimonies and says they will seek God with their whole heart. Deuteronomy promises that the scattered people will find the Lord when they seek Him with all their heart and soul in distress; the shared wholehearted seeking does not identify the psalm’s circumstances with that dispersion.

relationship: Commanded diligence in keeping commandments
rationale: The psalm says God commanded His commandments to be kept diligently. Deuteronomy directly commands diligent keeping of the Lord’s commandments, testimonies and ordinances, providing a close formulation of the obligation acknowledged in the poem.

relationship: Divine direction of a person’s way and steps
rationale: The speaker wishes that his ways might be directed to keep God’s ordinances. Psalm 36 states that a person’s steps are directed by the Lord; the desired direction in Psalm 118 is expressly toward obedience, while the target states the Lord’s direction of the person’s steps.

relationship: Obedience and freedom from shame (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 6 anticipates not being ashamed when looking to all the commandments. Verse 80 asks for a blameless heart in the ordinances so as not to be ashamed. The later petition returns to the earlier connection between attention to all commandments or a blameless heart in ordinances and freedom from shame.

relationship: Learning instruction followed by praise (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 7 promises upright-hearted thanksgiving when the speaker learns God’s righteous judgments. Verse 171 similarly asks that a hymn pour from the lips when God teaches His ordinances. The two passages expressly connect learning or being taught with the ensuing praise, while distinguishing heart and lips.

relationship: Words kept inwardly and a young person’s directed way
rationale: The psalm asks how a younger man can set his way right and answers with keeping God’s words. Proverbs addresses a son, commands attention to words and their keeping in the heart, and then commands straight tracks and avoidance of an evil way. Its final native continuation says God will make the tracks straight; the parental instruction is compared without identifying the two speakers.

relationship: Divine instruction in the heart guards conduct
rationale: Psalm 118 hides God’s sayings in the heart so as not to sin against Him. Psalm 36 places God’s law in the righteous person’s heart and says his steps will not be tripped up. Both connect inwardly held instruction with guarded conduct, using sin and stumbling respectively.

relationship: Commanded words placed in the heart
rationale: The speaker’s hiding of God’s sayings in his heart corresponds to Deuteronomy’s command that the words be in the hearer’s heart and soul. Psalm 118 adds the particular purpose of not sinning against God; Deuteronomy continues with teaching and speaking the words in daily life.

relationship: Divine instruction valued against material riches
rationale: The speaker delighted in the way of God’s testimonies as in all wealth. Psalm 18 calls the Lord’s judgments desirable beyond gold and much precious stone. Both explicitly compare the value of divine instruction with riches, while one speaks of delight as in wealth and the other of greater desirability.

relationship: Opened perception for understanding sacred writings
rationale: The psalm asks God to uncover the speaker’s eyes to consider wonders from His law. Luke says Jesus opened the disciples’ mind to understand the Scriptures after naming the Law of Moses, Prophets and Psalms. Opened eyes and opened mind are distinct images of enabled understanding; no identification of the psalm’s speaker with the disciples is required.

relationship: Earthly life described as sojourning before God
rationale: The speaker calls himself a sojourner on earth while asking that the commandments not be hidden. David’s prayer in Chronicles calls the people resident strangers and sojourners before God and compares their earthly days to a shadow. The common sojourner description is retained without assigning David as this psalm’s speaker.

relationship: A curse upon departure from divine instruction
rationale: The psalm calls those turning away from God’s commandments accursed and mentions His rebuke of the arrogant. Deuteronomy pronounces a curse upon everyone who does not continue in all the law’s words to do them. Both attach the curse to failure to remain with the commanded instruction.

relationship: Removal of reproach requested twice (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 22 asks that reproach and contempt be removed because the speaker sought the testimonies. Verse 39 returns to removal of dreaded reproach and declares the judgments good. The repeated request is compared with its different stated grounds, without treating either petition as an accomplished removal.

relationship: Rulers’ opposition beside attention to divine words (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 23 sets rulers sitting and speaking against the speaker beside his pondering of God’s ordinances. Verse 161 sets rulers’ causeless pursuit beside the heart’s fear of God’s words. The paired scenes contrast rulers’ opposition with the speaker’s response to divine instruction, without identifying the rulers or equating speaking against with pursuit.

relationship: Instruction serving as counsel and a speaking companion
rationale: The psalm calls the testimonies its meditation and the ordinances its counsels. Proverbs tells the son to retain parental laws and ordinances and presents instruction as a companion that accompanies, guards and converses with him. The comparison concerns instruction’s advisory role while preserving Proverbs’ parental setting.

relationship: Clinging to the ground in lament
rationale: Psalm 118 says the speaker’s soul clung to the ground and asks for life according to God’s word. Psalm 43 says the people’s soul was humbled to dust and their belly clung to the earth. The shared ground-clinging lament differs in its bodily subject and in singular versus communal voice.

relationship: Understanding and consideration of wonders in instruction (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 27 asks for understanding of the ordinances’ way and promises pondering of God’s wonders. Verse 18 asks for uncovered eyes to consider wonders from the law. Both petitions seek enabled comprehension of wonders, with understanding and uncovered eyes as distinct formulations.

relationship: Weariness answered with renewed strength
rationale: The psalm describes a soul dripping away from weariness and asks strengthening through God’s words. Isaiah contrasts young men growing weary and chosen men lacking strength with those enduring for God exchanging strength and running without weariness. The comparison concerns weariness and renewed strength; it does not substitute the familiar but absent wording about giving strength to the weary in Isaiah 40:29.

relationship: Two objects of clinging in the Delth stanza (same-chapter)
rationale: Within the same stanza, verse 25 says the soul clung to the ground, whereas verse 31 says the speaker clung to the testimonies. The repeated clinging language shifts from a condition prompting the plea for life to adherence prompting the plea against shame; the objects and petitions remain distinct.

relationship: Divine enlargement or abundance of heart
rationale: The speaker reports running in the commandments’ way when God enlarged his heart. First Kings says the Lord gave Solomon discernment, wisdom and abundance of heart like the sand beside the sea. Both describe divinely given expansiveness of heart, but the poem concerns running in obedience and the account concerns Solomon’s wisdom.

relationship: Teaching the divine way
rationale: Psalm 118 asks the Lord to instruct the speaker in the way of His ordinances and says he will seek it continually. Psalm 24 asks the Lord to make His ways known and teach His paths. The common formulation joins divine teaching with way or path imagery; the psalm’s continually seeking the ordinances is not supplied to the target.

relationship: The heart’s direction toward instruction or greed
rationale: The speaker asks God to bend his heart toward the testimonies and not greed. Jeremiah condemns eyes and heart directed toward greed, innocent blood and wrongdoing. The texts contrast the requested turning away from greed with an explicitly greedy orientation, without identifying the psalmist with Jeremiah’s addressee.

relationship: Turning the eyes from futility or lawlessness
rationale: Psalm 118 asks God to turn the eyes away from seeing futility. Psalm 100 reports not setting a lawless matter before the eyes. Both concern what is placed before one’s sight, while distinguishing futility from lawlessness and a petition from reported conduct.

relationship: Establishing the word spoken for the servant
rationale: The psalm asks God to establish His saying for His servant, for fear of Him. David’s prayer in 2 Samuel asks that the word concerning the servant and his house be confirmed for ever. The servant-and-established-word formulation is shared; the poem does not name a house or identify its saying as the dynastic promise.

relationship: Reproach-removal refrain with differing grounds (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 39 asks that dreaded reproach be removed because God’s judgments are good. Verse 22 similarly asks removal of reproach and contempt after seeking the testimonies. The repeated appeal is a literary link; the goodness of judgments and the speaker’s seeking are different stated grounds.

relationship: Mercy and salvation requested together
rationale: Psalm 118 asks for God’s mercy to come and for salvation according to His saying. Psalm 84 asks the Lord to show mercy and give salvation. Both petitions explicitly pair mercy with salvation, without turning either request into a report of completed rescue.

relationship: An answer grounded in hope amid reproach
rationale: The psalm anticipates answering reproachers with a word because the speaker hoped in God’s words. First Peter urges readiness to give an account of hope and joins that defense with good conscience under slander. The psalm’s reproachers and the letter’s questioners are not equated; the comparison joins hopeful speech with a context of hostile accusation.

relationship: Divine words remaining in the mouth
rationale: Psalm 118 asks that the word of truth not be removed utterly from the speaker’s mouth. Isaiah’s covenant declaration says the words put in the mouth will never fail from that mouth or the offspring’s mouth. The requested retention and promised persistence share the concrete mouth-and-word formulation, while Isaiah expressly extends it to offspring.

relationship: Walking or being brought into spaciousness
rationale: The speaker reports walking in a broad place because he sought God’s commandments. Psalm 17 reports God bringing the speaker into a spacious place and adds future rescue from enemies. The spacious-place image is shared; Psalm 118 grounds its walking in seeking commandments and does not itself narrate the target’s rescue event.

relationship: Testimony spoken before kings
rationale: The speaker reports speaking God’s testimonies before kings without shame. Jesus tells His messengers they will be brought before governors and kings as a testimony and that speech will be supplied to them. Both put testimony in a royal audience, with different speakers and past versus future settings.

relationship: Lifted hands in relation to divine commandments or name
rationale: The speaker raised his hands toward the commandments he loved. Psalm 62 promises to lift hands in God’s name. The shared raised-hand gesture is particular, but the different expressions toward commandments and in the name are preserved rather than treated as identical objects.

relationship: Life sustained amid humiliation (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 50 recalls comfort in humiliation because God’s saying gave life. Verse 92 says that without the law as meditation the speaker would have perished in humiliation. The two verses connect the same condition with life-preserving divine instruction, using a completed benefit and a counterfactual respectively.

relationship: Arrogant lawlessness contrasted with fidelity (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 51 says the arrogant acted lawlessly to excess while the speaker did not turn from the law. Verse 69 says the injustice of the arrogant multiplied against him, but he will search out the commandments with his whole heart. The repeated opponent-and-response pattern preserves the different forms of the speaker’s fidelity.

relationship: Earlier revelation as a source of comfort
rationale: The speaker remembered God’s judgments of old and was comforted. Romans says what was written beforehand serves instruction so that perseverance and the encouragement of the Scriptures might bring hope. Both connect earlier revelation with present encouragement, without asserting Romans quotes this verse.

relationship: Distress at the forsaking of divine commandments
rationale: Psalm 118 reports despondency because sinners forsake God’s law. Ezra’s account reports agitation and torn garments at covenant-breaking, then confesses that the community abandoned God’s commandments. The emotional responses and circumstances differ; the link is specifically distress over abandoned divine instruction, not identification of the two crises.

relationship: Song in sojourning or foreign land
rationale: Psalm 118 calls God’s ordinances songs in the place of the speaker’s sojourning. Psalm 136 reports captors demanding Zion’s songs and asks how to sing the Lord’s song on foreign land. Both join song with sojourning or life on foreign land, but Psalm 118 does not name captivity and reports songs where Psalm 136 voices a difficulty.

relationship: Remembrance during the night and dawn meditation
rationale: The speaker remembered God’s name at night and kept His law. Psalm 62 speaks conditionally of remembering God upon the bed and meditating on Him in the dawn hours. Both connect remembrance with these hours, while the name-and-law formulation is distinguished from remembrance of God upon the bed.

relationship: The Lord as the speaker’s portion
rationale: Psalm 118 declares the Lord to be the speaker’s portion and reports having said that he would keep the law. Psalm 15 calls the Lord the portion of the speaker’s inheritance and cup and the restorer of his inheritance. The shared portion language is retained without flattening the target’s fuller inheritance-and-cup expression.

relationship: Heart and face in seeking divine favor
rationale: Psalm 118 says the speaker entreated God’s face with his whole heart and asks mercy according to the saying. Psalm 26 has the heart say that the speaker’s face sought God, then expresses future seeking of the Lord’s face and asks that it not be turned away. Both combine heart, face and appeal, with different requests and no claim of identical circumstances.

relationship: The feet redirected along a right way
rationale: The speaker considered God’s ways and turned his feet toward the testimonies. Proverbs commands straight tracks, right direction of ways and turning the foot from an evil way, then says God will straighten tracks. The comparison is the concrete direction of feet and ways, preserving the psalm’s completed turn and Proverbs’ instruction and promise.

relationship: Hostile cords as a trapping image
rationale: Psalm 118 says sinners’ cords entangled the speaker, though he did not forget the law. Psalm 139 describes the proud hiding a trap and stretching cords as traps for his feet. The shared hostile-cord image does not require the sinners and proud to be the same group or the trapping scenes to be one event.

relationship: Worship at midnight
rationale: The psalm speaks of rising at midnight to thank God for His righteous judgments. Acts places Paul and Silas praying and singing hymns to God about midnight in prison. Midnight worship is the particular link; Acts does not say they were reciting this psalm, and the psalm does not name a prison.

relationship: Chosen association with those who fear the Lord
rationale: The speaker calls himself a companion of all who fear God and of those who keep His commandments. Psalm 14 describes the acceptable sojourner as honoring those who fear the Lord. Companionship and honor are different forms of positive association with the explicitly named God-fearing group.

relationship: The earth full of the Lord’s mercy
rationale: Psalm 118 declares the earth full of God’s mercy before asking instruction. Psalm 32 uses the same earth-full-of-mercy declaration after saying the Lord loves mercy and judgment. The shared claim is distinct from the instructional petition added in Psalm 118.

relationship: Learning discipline and knowledge
rationale: Psalm 118 asks to be taught kindness, discipline and knowledge because the speaker trusted the commandments. Proverbs announces learning wisdom and discipline and giving perception and thought to a young child. The texts share an instructional concern with discipline and knowing, but their lists and the psalm’s stated trust are not made identical.

relationship: Affliction connected with learning obedience
rationale: The speaker says that before being humbled he did wrong and therefore kept God’s saying. Deuteronomy recalls God’s afflicting and testing the people to reveal whether they would keep His commandments, then compares His chastening to a father’s. The personal account of wrongdoing before humbling and keeping the saying is compared with the wilderness discipline without identifying the experiences.

relationship: Arrogant injustice and steadfast response (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 69 sets the injustice of the arrogant multiplying against the speaker beside his promised wholehearted search for the commandments. Verse 51 similarly opposes the arrogant’s excessive lawlessness to his not turning from the law. This is a repeated two-part opposition, rather than a claim that every reference to the arrogant describes one incident.

relationship: Milk and curdling applied to human subjects
rationale: Psalm 118 says the opponents’ heart curdled like milk. Job asks whether God milked him out like milk and curdled him like cheese in the formation of his body. The distinctive milk-and-curdling imagery is shared; bodily formation is not equated with the psalm’s description of the opponents’ heart, nor is fatness substituted for curdling.

relationship: A painful experience described as beneficial training
rationale: The speaker says it was good to be humbled so that he might learn the ordinances. Hebrews describes divine discipline as beneficial for sharing holiness and says it yields righteousness after present sorrow. The shared beneficial-training pattern does not turn every affliction into punishment or identify the two experiences.

relationship: Divine instruction preferred to precious wealth
rationale: Psalm 118 values the law of God’s mouth above thousands of gold and silver. Psalm 18 calls God’s judgments desirable beyond gold and much precious stone. Both explicitly rank instruction above precious wealth, while retaining the psalm’s thousands and silver and the target’s precious stone.

relationship: God’s hands forming the person who prays
rationale: Psalm 118 says God’s hands made and formed the speaker and asks understanding to learn commandments. Job likewise addresses God as the One whose hands molded and made him, but then accuses Him of changing and striking him. The formation-by-hands language is shared while the contrasting ensuing appeals remain distinct.

relationship: Others’ rejoicing in connection with the speaker
rationale: Psalm 118 expects those fearing God to see the speaker and rejoice because he hoped in God’s words. Psalm 33 says the speaker’s soul will be praised in the Lord and invites the meek to hear and rejoice. Seeing and hearing, and those fearing God and the meek, remain distinct in this comparison of the speaker with others’ rejoicing.

relationship: God’s humbling and the keeping of commandments
rationale: Psalm 118 acknowledges righteous judgments and says God humbled the speaker in truth. Deuteronomy attributes the wilderness affliction and testing to God and explicitly connects it with whether the people would keep commandments. The shared divine humbling is interpreted within each text’s own setting, not as proof the psalm narrates the wilderness.

relationship: Comfort requested after comfort remembered (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 76 asks for mercy as comfort according to God’s saying to His servant. Verse 50 remembers being comforted in humiliation because the saying gave life. The later request echoes the earlier reported comfort and common appeal to the saying, without turning the request itself into a completed event.

relationship: The God-fearing community and the speaker (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 79 asks those fearing God, and those knowing the testimonies, to turn toward the speaker. Verse 63 calls him a companion of those fearing God and of those keeping commandments. The paired descriptions are related to the speaker through requested turning and declared companionship; knowing and keeping are distinguished, and identical membership of the groups is not asserted.

relationship: Blamelessness in way and heart (same-chapter)
rationale: The opening verse blesses those blameless in their way who walk in the law. Verse 80 asks for a blameless heart in the ordinances so as not to be ashamed. The petition applies the opening blamelessness motif inwardly, distinguishing a blessed way from a requested condition of the heart.

relationship: Longing for salvation beside attention to instruction (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 81 describes the soul failing in longing for salvation while hoping in God’s word. Verse 174 again declares longing for salvation and calls the law the speaker’s meditation. The repeated longing-for-salvation formulation has different accompanying responses, and only verse 81 describes the failing soul.

relationship: Eyes failing while awaiting the divine saying (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 82 says the eyes failed in longing for God’s saying and asks when comfort will come. Verse 123 repeats the failing-eyes image in longing for salvation and the righteous saying. The bodily image and awaited saying recur, with comfort and salvation distinguished.

relationship: Wineskin similes with differing physical conditions
rationale: Psalm 118 compares the speaker to a wineskin in frost while he does not forget the ordinances. Job 13:28 says that it grows old like a wineskin or moth-eaten garment. The comparison is the unusual wineskin simile; it preserves frost versus aging and does not resolve the target’s pronoun or substitute smoke for frost.

relationship: True commandments beside approaching lawless pursuers (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 86 calls all commandments truth and asks help against unjust pursuit. Verses 150–151 set lawless pursuers drawing near, though far from the law, beside the Lord being near and all His commandments being truth. The repeated truth claim appears in both pursuit settings, with the later near-and-far contrast adding a distinct development.

relationship: Life and utterance from God’s mouth
rationale: Psalm 118 asks for life according to mercy and declares that the speaker will keep the testimonies of God’s mouth. Deuteronomy says a person lives by every word proceeding through God’s mouth. Both join life with divine utterance from the mouth, while the psalm combines a request for life with an undertaking to keep testimonies and Deuteronomy identifies that by which a person lives.

relationship: God’s word remaining for ever
rationale: Psalm 118 declares that God’s word remains for ever in heaven. Isaiah contrasts withered grass and fallen flower with the word of God remaining for ever. The same permanence claim is shared; the heavenly location and the grass-and-flower contrast belong to their respective passages.

relationship: Truth extending through generations
rationale: Psalm 118 declares God’s truth from generation to generation and joins it with the earth He founded remaining. Psalm 88 promises to proclaim His truth from generation to generation and reports God’s saying that truth will be prepared in the heavens. The generational truth expression is shared without equating the earthly and heavenly statements.

relationship: The day or morning ordered by God
rationale: Psalm 118 says the day remains by God’s arrangement and all things are His servants. In the Lord’s speech in Job, He asks whether He ordered morning brightness in Job’s time and describes the dawn-bearer’s appointed place. Both place daylight under divine ordering; the psalm’s all-things-as-servants claim is not inserted into Job’s question.

relationship: Instruction sustaining life under humiliation (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 92 says the speaker would have perished in humiliation without the law as meditation. Verse 50 recalls comfort in humiliation because God’s saying gave life. The counterfactual and remembered event share humiliation and life sustained through instruction, without being made one narrated occurrence.

relationship: Remembered instruction associated with life
rationale: Psalm 118 resolves never to forget the ordinances because God gave life through them. Proverbs commands attention to words and keeping them in the heart, explaining that there is life for those finding them and healing for all flesh. Both give life as a reason for retaining instruction, with divine ordinances and parental words distinguished.

relationship: Belonging to God and appeal to rescue
rationale: The speaker says he is God’s and asks to be saved, having sought the ordinances. Isaiah’s divine address to Jacob and Israel says God redeemed them, called by name and declared them His. The belonging-and-rescue connection is explicit in both, with petition and completed redemption, and individual and national address, distinguished.

relationship: A sinner’s watch directed toward another’s death
rationale: Psalm 118 says sinners waited to destroy the speaker while he understood the testimonies. Psalm 36 describes the sinner observing the righteous and seeking to put him to death. Waiting or observation directed toward killing is the particular parallel; no identity of the attackers is asserted.

relationship: Delight in the law and sustained meditation
rationale: Psalm 118 exclaims over love of the law and calls it meditation all day. Psalm 1 places the blessed person’s will in the Lord’s law and says he will meditate on it day and night. Both combine inward attachment with an explicitly sustained rhythm of meditation, preserving all day versus day and night.

relationship: Commandments and wisdom before others
rationale: Psalm 118 says God made the speaker wiser than enemies in His commandment. Deuteronomy tells Israel to keep and do the ordinances because this is their wisdom and understanding before other nations. Both connect commanded instruction with wisdom visible in relation to others, without equating enemies with all nations.

relationship: Comparative understanding beyond teachers and elders (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 99 says the speaker understood more than all his teachers because the testimonies are his meditation. Verse 100 similarly claims understanding beyond elders because he sought the commandments. The consecutive comparisons distinguish teachers from elders and meditation from seeking rather than treating those groups as identical.

relationship: Understanding not measured simply by age
rationale: Psalm 118 claims understanding beyond elders because the speaker sought commandments. Elihu recounts expecting years to convey wisdom, then says the Almighty’s breath teaches and that the long-lived are not wise and elders do not know judgment. Elihu’s speech is identified as his argument, not made the narrator’s unqualified verdict on the debate.

relationship: The foot restrained or turned from an evil way
rationale: Psalm 118 reports restraining the feet from every evil way to keep God’s words. Proverbs commands turning the foot away from an evil way and not turning right or left. The shared foot-and-evil-way language connects restraint with moral direction while preserving report and command.

relationship: Divine sayings sweeter than honey
rationale: Psalm 118 calls God’s sayings sweet to the throat beyond honey and honeycomb to the mouth. Psalm 18 likewise describes the Lord’s judgments as sweeter than honey and honeycomb. The distinctive double honey comparison is shared, with throat and mouth explicit in Psalm 118.

relationship: Divine utterance experienced as honey in the mouth
rationale: Psalm 118 describes God’s sayings as sweeter than honey to the mouth. Ezekiel reports eating the given scroll, which became like sweet honey in his mouth, before being sent to speak God’s words. Figurative sweetness of sayings and the narrated eating of a scroll remain distinct.

relationship: Commandments joined to hatred of the unjust way (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 104 derives understanding from commandments and therefore hatred of every unjust way. Verse 128 says the speaker was set right toward all commandments and hated every unjust way. The repeated rejection of the unjust way is paired with gaining understanding from commandments and being set right toward them, without assigning the latter phrase an unstated cause.

relationship: Instruction as lamp, light and a guide for the way
rationale: Psalm 118 calls God’s word a lamp for the feet and a light for paths. Proverbs calls the commandment of law a lamp and a light and associates correction and discipline with life’s way. The lamp-and-light image is shared, with feet and paths explicit in the psalm and life’s way in Proverbs.

relationship: The word compared with a shining lamp
rationale: Psalm 118 describes the word as a lamp for feet and light for paths. Second Peter compares attention to the prophetic word with attention to a lamp shining in a dark place until day dawns. The shared word-and-lamp image has different settings and does not turn the psalm’s path into the letter’s daybreak expectation.

relationship: An oath to keep divine judgments
rationale: The speaker says he swore and established an undertaking to keep God’s righteous judgments. The account in Nehemiah records entry into a curse and oath to walk in God’s law and keep His commandments and judgments. The oath-and-observance connection is explicit, while a personal resolution and communal undertaking remain distinct.

relationship: A plea for life beside remembered life in humiliation (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 107 describes extreme humiliation and asks for life according to God’s word. Verse 50 recalls comfort in humiliation because God’s saying gave life. The later petition repeats the earlier humiliation-and-life pattern, while completed comfort is not attributed to the current request.

relationship: Speech presented as an offering to God
rationale: Psalm 118 asks acceptance of the mouth’s freewill offerings. Hebrews urges offering through Jesus a sacrifice of praise, defined as fruit of lips confessing God’s name. Both present speech through an offering image; the freewill offerings are not made identical to the letter’s explicitly Christ-mediated sacrifice.

relationship: Life or soul in one’s own hand
rationale: Psalm 118 says the speaker’s soul is continually in his hands and says he did not forget the law. Jephthah reports putting his life in his hand when he crossed against Ammon without a deliverer. The distinctive hand-and-life expression is shared, with continual condition and a particular military action distinguished.

relationship: A trap laid by hostile people
rationale: Psalm 118 says sinners set a trap while the speaker did not wander from commandments. Psalm 139 describes the proud hiding a trap and setting cords and a stumbling block along the path. The concrete trap imagery connects the passages without supplying the target’s cords to Psalm 118:110 or identifying the hostile groups.

relationship: Divine instruction as an inheritance
rationale: The speaker inherited God’s testimonies for ever and calls them the heart’s rejoicing. Deuteronomy calls the law commanded by Moses an inheritance for Jacob’s assemblies. Both name instruction as inheritance, while the personal joy and perpetual possession are explicit only in the psalm.

relationship: Keeping instruction with recompense in view
rationale: Psalm 118 says the speaker bent his heart to perform ordinances for ever, for recompense. Psalm 18 says God’s servant keeps the judgments and that in keeping them there is great recompense. The shared keeping-and-recompense formulation preserves the psalm’s stated heart orientation and the target’s greatness of reward.

relationship: Hatred and love contrasted around the law (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 113 opposes hatred of lawbreakers to love of the law. Verse 163 opposes hatred and abhorrence of injustice to love of the law. The repeated contrast preserves the important difference between lawbreakers as persons and injustice as the object rejected.

relationship: A direct command that evildoers depart
rationale: Psalm 118 tells evildoers to turn away and declares that the speaker will search God’s commandments. Psalm 6 orders all workers of lawlessness to stand away because the Lord heard the weeping. The direct dismissal of wrongdoers is shared; the source joins it with a promised search, while the target grounds it in the hearing of weeping.

relationship: Expectation or hope not ending in shame
rationale: Psalm 118 asks to be upheld according to God’s saying and not be shamed in expectation. Romans states that hope does not put believers to shame because God’s love has been poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit. The expectation-and-shame connection is retained without equating the petition’s grounds with the letter’s stated explanation.

relationship: Divine rejection of those departing instruction (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 118 says God despised those departing His ordinances because their thought is unjust. Verse 21 reports rebuke of the arrogant and calls those turning away from commandments accursed. The shared departure from instruction and adverse divine response are compared while despising, rebuke and curse retain their distinct wording.

relationship: Flesh nailed down or crucified in distinct spiritual settings
rationale: Psalm 118 asks God to nail down the speaker’s flesh through fear of God, adding that he feared God’s judgments. Galatians says those belonging to Christ Jesus crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. The connection is the concrete fastening or crucifying image applied to flesh, not an assertion that the psalm names a cross or describes the same completed act.

relationship: Protection from false accusation (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 122 asks God to receive His servant for good and prevent the arrogant from oppressing him with false accusations. Verse 134 asks redemption from people’s oppression by false accusation and promises to keep commandments. The same specific hostile action prompts different protective requests; the people are not thereby proved to be one identified group.

relationship: The repeated image of eyes failing in longing (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 123 says the eyes failed in longing for salvation and God’s righteous saying. Verse 82 similarly says the eyes failed longing for the saying, then asks when comfort will come. The repeated bodily image and awaited saying connect the petitions while preserving their different expressed hopes.

relationship: Scattering divine law or commandments
rationale: Psalm 118 announces a time to act for the Lord and says that they scattered His law. Ezra’s prayer confesses that the community returned to scattering God’s commandments and intermarrying. The unusual scattering language for disobedience is shared; the poem does not identify its they with Ezra’s community or turn time to act for the Lord into a different supplied subject.

relationship: Instruction or wisdom valued above gold and topaz
rationale: Psalm 118 says the speaker loved the commandments above gold and topaz. Job’s wisdom poem says Ethiopian topazion cannot equal wisdom and pure gold cannot be weighed with it. The gold-and-topaz comparison is particular, while commandments and wisdom and the target’s qualifiers remain distinct.

relationship: A repeated rejection of every unjust way (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 128 joins being set right toward all commandments with hatred of every unjust way. Verse 104 joins understanding through the commandments with the same hatred of every unjust way. The explicit repeated conclusion makes the link, without collapsing set right into understood.

relationship: Wonders in instruction prompting inquiry (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 129 calls the testimonies wonderful and therefore says the soul searched them. Verse 18 asks for uncovered eyes to consider wonders from the law. The wonderful character of instruction is linked with searching or enabled consideration, while testimony and law retain their terms.

relationship: Instruction giving light and understanding to the simple
rationale: Psalm 118 says the disclosure of God’s words will give light and understanding to the simple. Psalm 18 calls the testimony trustworthy and making infants wise, and the commandment shining and giving light to eyes. The combined light-and-understanding pattern is explicit, without equating simple people exactly with infants.

relationship: A plea or assurance against sin’s dominion
rationale: Psalm 118 asks for directed steps according to God’s saying and that no lawlessness rule over the speaker. Romans says sin will not rule over the addressees because they are under grace rather than law. The dominion language is shared, but petition and assurance and their different stated grounds are preserved.

relationship: The Lord’s direction of steps
rationale: Psalm 118 asks God to direct the steps according to His saying and prevent lawlessness from ruling. Psalm 36 states that a person’s steps are directed by the Lord. The common Lord-directed steps image does not supply the psalm’s explicit protection from lawlessness to the target.

relationship: Two requests concerning false accusation (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 134 asks redemption from people’s oppression by false accusation and promises that the speaker will keep commandments. Verse 122 asks that the arrogant not oppress God’s servant with false accusations. The specific oppression-through-false-accusation wording recurs, distinguishing rescue from prevention and people from the arrogant.

relationship: The shining divine face in blessing and petition
rationale: Psalm 118 asks God to make His face shine upon His servant and teach ordinances. The priestly blessing in Numbers asks that the Lord make His face shine upon the recipient and have mercy. The same shining-face formulation connects the personal petition with the prescribed blessing, without equating their recipients or added requests.

relationship: God’s face shining upon His servant
rationale: Both passages ask God to make His face shine upon His servant. Psalm 118 adds instruction in ordinances, whereas Psalm 30 adds salvation in mercy. The exact face-and-servant petition is preserved with those different accompanying requests.

relationship: Water pouring from the eye in grief
rationale: Psalm 118 describes streams from the eyes because they did not keep God’s law. Lamentations says the eye will bring down outpourings of water at the shattering of the daughter of the people. Both use abundant water from the eye for grief, distinguishing disobedience from devastation and reported streams from the target’s future outpouring.

relationship: Truth and righteousness attributed to divine judgments
rationale: Psalm 118 says God commanded His testimonies as righteousness and exceeding truth. Psalm 18 calls the Lord’s judgments true and justified together. The paired truth-and-righteousness description connects the instruction terms without converting testimonies into a quotation of the target.

relationship: Zeal for God’s house consuming or melting the speaker
rationale: Psalm 118 says zeal for God’s house melted the speaker because enemies forgot God’s words. Psalm 68 says zeal for God’s house devoured the speaker and that reproaches against God fell on him. The distinctive house-zeal and consuming effect are shared, with melting and devouring and the accompanying statements distinguished.

relationship: House-zeal language recalled around Jesus’ temple action
rationale: Psalm 118 uses zeal for God’s house with a melting effect on the speaker. John records the disciples remembering the written saying that zeal for God’s house will consume Jesus. The shared house-zeal formulation is compared without claiming John expressly quotes Psalm 118 rather than the closer wording of Psalm 68:10.

relationship: Divine sayings refined by fire
rationale: Psalm 118 calls God’s saying thoroughly refined by fire and loved by the servant. Psalm 11 describes the Lord’s sayings as pure, like silver tried by fire and purified sevenfold. The refining image is shared; silver and sevenfold purification belong explicitly to Psalm 11.

relationship: God’s words refined by fire
rationale: Psalm 118 describes God’s saying as thoroughly fire-refined. Proverbs states that all God’s words have been refined by fire and adds His shielding of those who revere Him. The close fire-refining statement stands without supplying the target’s shielding clause to the source.

relationship: Youth, contempt and fidelity in conduct
rationale: Psalm 118 describes the speaker as younger and despised and says he did not forget the ordinances. First Timothy tells its recipient not to let anyone despise his youth and to be a pattern in word and conduct. The youth-and-contempt conjunction is specific, with reported contempt and an exhortation against it distinguished.

relationship: Divine law or word expressly called truth
rationale: Psalm 118 says God’s righteousness lasts for ever and His law is truth. Jesus’ prayer in John asks sanctification in truth and declares the Father’s word truth. The direct truth predication is shared, while law, word, lasting righteousness and sanctification retain their different textual roles.

relationship: Law as meditation amid distress (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 143 sets affliction and constraint finding the speaker beside the commandments as his meditation. Verse 92 says that without the law as meditation he would have perished in humiliation. The recurrent conjunction of distress and sustaining meditation is compared, without attributing the latter counterfactual to verse 143 itself.

relationship: Rising unusually early for prayer
rationale: Psalm 118 reports rising early at an untimely hour and crying out, and says the speaker placed hope in God’s words. Mark says Jesus rose very early while it was still dark, went to a deserted place and prayed. Unusually early rising with prayer is shared; the psalm does not specify Jesus, a deserted place or the target’s darkness.

relationship: Dawn hours and meditation
rationale: Psalm 118 says the eyes were awake before dawn to meditate on God’s sayings. Psalm 62 conditionally connects remembering God upon the bed with meditation on Him in the dawn hours. The timing-and-meditation conjunction is specific, while before dawn and during dawn hours, and sayings and God Himself, remain distinct.

relationship: Near pursuers, distant law and the near Lord (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 150 says lawless pursuers drew near although they were far from God’s law. Verse 151 immediately declares the Lord near and His commandments truth. The consecutive near-and-far contrast opposes threatening proximity to divine proximity without saying the Lord or the pursuers have the same relation to the law.

relationship: The near Lord contrasted with near lawless pursuers (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 151 declares God near and all His commandments truth. The preceding verse describes pursuers drawing near but being far from His law. These adjacent statements differentiate physical or threatening nearness from fidelity to instruction and the asserted nearness of God.

relationship: Testimonies or commandments established for ever
rationale: Psalm 118 says from the beginning the speaker knew from God’s testimonies that He established them for ever. Psalm 110 calls the commandments faithful, established for an age of an age and made in truth and uprightness. The shared establishment and permanence claim preserves the psalm’s personal from-the-beginning knowledge.

relationship: God asked to see the speaker’s humiliation
rationale: Psalm 118 asks God to see humiliation and rescue, adding that the speaker did not forget the law. Psalm 24 similarly asks God to see humiliation and toil but asks forgiveness of all sins. The repeated see-my-humiliation petition is linked while rescue and forgiveness and their surrounding professions remain distinct.

relationship: Divine adjudication of the speaker’s case and rescue
rationale: Psalm 118 asks God to judge the speaker’s case and redeem him, followed by a request for life because of the word. Psalm 42 asks God to judge the speaker’s case against an unholy nation and rescue him from an unjust, deceitful person. The judicial case-and-rescue appeal is shared without supplying the target’s specified opponents to the source.

relationship: Distance of salvation or God from the impious
rationale: Psalm 118 says salvation is far from sinners because they did not seek the ordinances. Proverbs says God is far distant from the impious but hears righteous people’s prayers. Both use distance for the impious person’s relation to divine help, with salvation and God as the respective grammatical subjects.

relationship: Melting in response to neglected divine words (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 158 says the speaker saw people breaking faith and melted because they did not keep God’s sayings. Verse 139 says zeal for God’s house melted him because enemies forgot the words. The repeated melting and others’ neglect of divine speech link the passages, with seeing breach of faith and zeal for the house distinguished.

relationship: Truth predicated of divine speech
rationale: Psalm 118 says the beginning of God’s words is truth and all His righteous judgments last for ever. Jesus’ prayer declares the Father’s word truth. The comparison preserves beginning rather than substituting sum or totality, and does not make John’s statement include the psalm’s everlasting-judgments clause.

relationship: Royal pursuit answered with a claim of innocence
rationale: Psalm 118 says rulers pursued the speaker without cause while his heart feared God’s words. David tells Saul he has done no evil or sin against him and asks whom the king is pursuing. The comparison concerns royal pursuit asserted to be unjust; it does not identify this anonymous psalm’s speaker as David or its rulers as Saul.

relationship: Joy compared with obtaining or dividing spoil
rationale: Psalm 118 anticipates rejoicing over God’s sayings like one finding much spoil. Isaiah compares the people’s future rejoicing with harvest rejoicing and those dividing spoils. The distinctive spoil-and-joy comparison is shared, while finding and dividing and the different occasions remain distinct.

relationship: Law loved beside hatred of differing objects (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 163 says the speaker hated and abhorred injustice but loved the law. Verse 113 says he hated lawbreakers but loved the law. The repeated contrast distinguishes hatred of injustice from hatred of lawbreakers rather than silently equating an act with people.

relationship: Timed praise because of righteous judgments (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 164 reports praise seven times in the day because of righteous judgments. Verse 62 speaks of rising at midnight to thank God because of righteous judgments. The recurring reason and specified times make the link, without adding the two statements into an unstated numerical schedule.

relationship: Peace associated with regard for commandments
rationale: Psalm 118 declares great peace for those loving God’s law. Isaiah says that if the addressee had listened to God’s commands, peace would have become like a river. The law-and-peace connection is shared while the psalm’s declaration and Isaiah’s counterfactual are kept distinct.

relationship: Divine law and the absence of stumbling
rationale: Psalm 118 says those loving God’s law have great peace and no stumbling block. Psalm 36 places God’s law in the righteous person’s heart and says his steps will not be tripped up. Love of law and law in the heart are related through the explicit absence-of-stumbling image, not treated as identical statements.

relationship: All human ways before God
rationale: Psalm 118 says the speaker kept commandments and testimonies because all his ways are before God. Proverbs says a man’s ways are before God’s eyes and He watches all his tracks. The shared all-seeing relation to human ways is particular; the psalm’s obedience and Proverbs’ warning context remain distinct.

relationship: Praise arising when instruction is learned (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 171 asks that lips pour out a hymn when God teaches ordinances. Verse 7 promises upright-hearted thanksgiving when the speaker learns righteous judgments. The matching when-taught-or-learned structure frames praise as a response to instruction, without asserting the two acts of praise already occurred.

relationship: Tongue speaking judgment or divine saying
rationale: Psalm 118 asks that the tongue utter God’s saying and declares all His commandments righteousness. Psalm 36 says the righteous person’s mouth will meditate on wisdom and his tongue will speak judgment. The explicit tongue-and-just-speech pattern is shared while a divine saying and the righteous person’s judgment are distinguished.

relationship: Repeated longing for salvation (same-chapter)
rationale: Verse 174 declares longing for God’s salvation and identifies the law as meditation. Verse 81 describes the soul failing while longing for salvation and hoping in the word. The repeated longing is linked with two different responses to instruction, and the failing-soul condition is confined to verse 81.

relationship: Living and praising God
rationale: Psalm 118 anticipates the soul living and praising God, and God’s judgments helping the speaker. Psalm 113 contrasts the dead and those descending to Hades, who will not praise, with the living who will bless the Lord. The explicit life-and-praise connection is shared without making Psalm 118 itself state the target’s description of the dead.

relationship: The wandering or lost sheep sought by God
rationale: The psalm ends with the speaker as a lost sheep asking God to seek His servant, while professing not to forget commandments. Ezekiel has God promise to seek the lost and bring back the wandering among His sheep. The shared seeking-and-lost-sheep pattern does not erase the psalm’s statement that the speaker did not forget commandments.

relationship: Seeking and finding a lost sheep
rationale: Psalm 118 asks God to seek the speaker who wandered like a lost sheep. Jesus’ parable describes going after a lost sheep until finding it and interprets the joy in relation to a repentant sinner. The common search image is retained without importing the whole parable’s repentance framework into the psalm’s profession of remembered commandments.

relationship: Human wandering described through sheep
rationale: Psalm 118 describes the speaker as wandering like a lost sheep. Isaiah describes all of us as sheep gone astray, each in his own way, before speaking of the Lord delivering the suffering figure over to our sins. The shared sheep-and-wandering image is limited to that comparison; the psalm’s servant is not identified with Isaiah’s suffering figure.

relationship: Wandering sheep and return to a shepherd
rationale: Psalm 118 asks God to seek the wandering speaker pictured as a lost sheep. First Peter describes the addressees as formerly wandering sheep who have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls. The psalm requests seeking, whereas the letter reports a completed return; neither is turned into the other’s chronology.
